sources: MacCulloch, J. A. The Religion of the Ancient Celts. London: Constable, 1911, 57, 80.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The Celts entered history as migratory herding tribes. They soon took up farming, perhaps from contact with settled peoples. New religious rites grew to support the new lifestyle. The rites may have been Celtic inventions or adaptations from pre-Celtic cultures. In Ireland, some rituals linked with herding, such as driving animals between the Beltane fires. Others linked with farming. People offered fruits to the god Crom Dubh at Samhain. Together they show a mixed economy. Irish myths also held that the king was married to the goddess of the region, and that her fertility relied on his actions. In Wales, the god Amaethon appears in the epic poem Kulhwch and Olwen as a human farmer who made barren wastelands bloom. The rituals offered to him were not recorded.

okr.objective: Record the farming and herding rituals of the Celts.
key_results: Show the mixed economy of Ireland, the king bond to the goddess, and the Welsh god Amaethon.
